title: Fuel system and bleeding
summary: How fuel gets from the tank to the injectors, keeping it clean and free of water, and how to bleed out air when the engine is starved.

lessons.title: From tank to injector
lessons.intro: A diesel engine is fussy about its fuel. It needs a steady supply, free of air, water and dirt, delivered to the injectors at very high pressure. Following the fuel's path from the tank to the cylinders makes most fuel problems much easier to understand.

diagram.caption: One example layout on a mechanically injected engine. Yours may have the parts in a different order or combine some of them, and a common-rail engine has a high-pressure pump and rail in place of the injection pump.

labels.title: Fuel tank
labels.detail: With a filler, a vent and a pick-up pipe that draws from just above the bottom.

labels.title: Shut-off valve
labels.detail: Lets you stop the fuel at the tank, for example to change a filter or in a fire.

labels.title: Primary filter and water separator
labels.detail: Catches water and larger dirt. Often has a clear bowl and a drain.

labels.title: Lift pump
labels.detail: Draws fuel from the tank and pushes it on at low pressure.

labels.title: Engine fine filter
labels.detail: Removes the small particles that would damage the injection equipment.

labels.title: Injection pump
labels.detail: Raises the fuel to a very high pressure and times its delivery.

labels.title: Injectors
labels.detail: Spray a fine mist of fuel into each cylinder. Spare fuel returns to the tank.

diagram.description: A flow diagram of a typical fuel system in seven stages: the fuel tank, the shut-off valve, the primary filter and water separator, the lift pump, the engine fine filter, the injection pump and the injectors, with spare fuel returning to the tank.

steps.title: The tank
steps.text: Fuel is drawn through a pick-up pipe that stops a little above the bottom of the tank, so that water and sludge which settle there are less likely to be drawn in. The tank also needs a vent so air can replace the fuel that is used.

steps.title: The low-pressure side
steps.text: In one common layout, fuel passes from the tank through a shut-off valve and a primary filter to the lift pump, then through a finer filter mounted on the engine. The order and number of filters vary between installations. Everything up to the injection pump works at low pressure, and much of it is under suction. A small leak on the suction side lets air in rather than letting fuel out.

steps.title: The high-pressure side
steps.text: On a mechanically injected engine, the injection pump raises the fuel to a very high pressure and sends a measured amount along a separate steel pipe to each injector at exactly the right moment. On a common-rail engine, a high-pressure pump keeps fuel in a shared rail and electronically controlled injectors take it from there. Either way, the high-pressure side is not for owner work.

steps.title: The return line
steps.text: The injection system is supplied with more fuel than it burns. The spare fuel, along with any air it has picked up, goes back to the tank through a return or leak-off line.

steps.title: Why air is the enemy
steps.text: Air in the fuel compresses instead of building pressure, so the injection pump cannot deliver fuel properly. Even a small bubble can stop the engine. That is why the fuel system has to be bled after it has been opened or allowed to run dry.

lessons.reviewNote: Audit note 4, revise (S14): the fuel path is now presented as one example configuration; the text says filter and lift-pump order vary, and the high-pressure side covers common rail. Please approve.

lessons.title: Filters and water separation
lessons.intro: Clean fuel is the single most important thing you can give a diesel engine. Two stages of filtering protect the expensive injection equipment, and the first stage also traps water before it can do harm.
lessons.caution: Diesel is slippery and irritates the skin. Wear gloves, mop up spills straight away, and never let fuel go into the bilge where it could be pumped overboard. No naked flames or smoking while the fuel system is open.

steps.title: Why filtering matters
steps.text: The injection pump and injectors are made to extremely fine tolerances. Particles too small to see, or a drop of water, can wear them, make them stick or stop the engine altogether.

steps.title: The primary filter
steps.text: The first filter, usually mounted between the tank and the engine, catches larger dirt and separates water from the fuel. Water is heavier than diesel, so it sinks to the bottom of the filter bowl, where you can often see it as a separate layer.

steps.title: The engine fine filter
steps.text: The second filter, usually on the engine itself, removes much smaller particles. It should only ever see fuel that has already been through the primary filter.

steps.title: Checking and draining water
steps.text: With the engine stopped, look at the primary filter bowl. If you see water or dirt at the bottom, open the drain into a container until clean fuel runs out, then close it firmly. Make this part of your regular checks, and check again after rough weather or taking on fuel from an unfamiliar source.

steps.title: Changing filters
steps.text: Filter elements are changed at the intervals in your engine handbook, or sooner if they block. Close the fuel valve, have rags and a container ready, and fit new seals with each element. Afterwards, the system will usually need bleeding or priming to remove the air let in; common-rail engines often have their own priming method in the handbook.

steps.title: Carry spares
steps.text: Keep at least one spare element for each filter, with their seals, on board. A blocked filter can stop an engine at sea, often at an awkward moment.

lessons.reviewNote: S14: filter changes now mention common-rail priming, and the 'one of the most common reasons' claim is removed. Please approve.

lessons.title: Lift pump, injection pump and injectors
lessons.intro: Several components move the fuel through the engine. Knowing what each one does helps you understand why the low-pressure side is something an owner can work on, while the high-pressure side is for a qualified engineer.
lessons.caution: Fuel in high-pressure pipes and rails is at a pressure high enough to pierce skin and cause serious injury. Never feel for a leak with your hand, and do not loosen any high-pressure fuel connection: that work is for a qualified engineer.

steps.title: The lift pump
steps.text: The lift pump draws fuel from the tank and pushes it through the fine filter to the injection pump. Many are driven mechanically by the engine and have a small hand lever, which you use when bleeding the system. Some engines use an electric lift pump instead.

steps.title: The injection pump (mechanical injection)
steps.text: The injection pump is the heart of the fuel system. Driven by the engine, it raises the fuel to a very high pressure, meters the amount for each cylinder according to the throttle, and times each delivery to the position of the pistons.

steps.title: The injectors
steps.text: Each injector holds a spring-loaded valve that opens only when the fuel pressure is high enough. The fuel then sprays through tiny holes as a fine mist, which mixes with the hot air and burns quickly and cleanly.

steps.title: Common-rail systems
steps.text: Many newer engines use common-rail injection. A high-pressure pump keeps fuel in a shared rail at a far higher pressure than older systems, sensors report what the engine is doing, and an electronic control unit opens each injector. Owners can do low-pressure jobs such as changing filters and draining water where the handbook allows, but nothing on the high-pressure side: that is for trained technicians with the right equipment.

steps.title: Signs of injector trouble
steps.text: A worn or sticking injector may give black smoke, a knock from one cylinder, rough running or hard starting. Injectors are tested and serviced with special equipment, so suspected injector faults are a job for a specialist.

steps.title: The stop control
steps.text: Many mechanically injected diesels are stopped by cutting off the fuel at the injection pump, with a pull cable or an electric solenoid. Electronically controlled engines are usually stopped through the key switch or control panel. If a stop cable is not fully returned, the engine may crank but refuse to start.

Please approve.

lessons.title: Bleeding the fuel system
lessons.intro: If air gets into the fuel system, the engine will not start or will run briefly and stop. Bleeding means pushing fuel through the low-pressure side until all the air has been driven out. This lesson describes a typical mechanically injected engine; your handbook gives the exact points and order for yours, and common-rail engines usually have their own priming procedure.
lessons.caution: Avoid long periods of cranking while bleeding: it flattens the battery and overheats the starter. Wear gloves and keep naked flames away while the fuel system is open.

steps.title: When you need to bleed
steps.text: After running out of fuel, after changing a fuel filter, after any part of the fuel system has been disconnected, or when air has been drawn in through a leak. Find and fix the cause first, or the air will come back.

steps.title: Get ready
steps.text: Make sure there is fuel in the tank and the fuel valve is open, and that the engine cannot be started accidentally while you work. Have the right spanners, plenty of rags and a small container. Lay rags under each bleed point to catch fuel.

steps.title: Work from the tank towards the engine
steps.text: Start at the bleed point nearest the tank and work along the fuel's path. Bleeding further along first just pulls more air through from behind.

steps.title: Pump until the bubbles stop
steps.text: Open the first bleed screw a little and operate the lift pump's hand lever, or switch on an electric lift pump. Keep pumping until fuel comes out with no bubbles, then close the screw while fuel is still flowing. Move on to the next bleed point and repeat.

steps.title: If the hand lever feels dead
steps.text: On a cam-operated mechanical lift pump, the engine's cam can leave the lever with little travel. Turning the engine a little, in the way your handbook describes, usually brings the lever back to life. Electric lift pumps have no lever and do not have this problem.

steps.title: Finishing off
steps.text: Some engines bleed themselves once the low-pressure side is full. Others need further bleeding at the injection pump, which the handbook describes for your engine. When the engine starts, let it run and watch for leaks at every point you opened, then clean up all spilt fuel.

steps.title: If it still will not run
steps.text: Do not loosen injector pipes or any part of a common-rail system. If the handbook's owner procedure does not get the engine running, or your engine has no approved owner bleeding method, stop and get a qualified engineer.

lessons.reviewNote: Audit note 6, safety revise (P0, S02): warning B is now shown before the steps, verbatim, together with the wet-exhaust warning A for prolonged cranking. Instructions are limited to handbook-approved low-pressure bleeding, the reference to loosening injector pipes has been removed, and a final engineer-only step covers anything else. lessons.title: Diesel bug and fuel care
lessons.intro: Water in a fuel tank allows micro-organisms to grow where the fuel and water meet. The result, usually called diesel bug, is a dark slime that blocks filters, often at the worst possible moment.
lessons.caution: Some fuel additives are hazardous. Read the label, wear gloves, and never mix products unless the maker says you can.

steps.title: What diesel bug is
steps.text: Bacteria and fungi live in the thin layer where water meets fuel at the bottom of a tank. They feed on the fuel and form a dark, slimy sludge, and they can produce acids that attack metal tanks.

steps.title: How water gets in
steps.text: Condensation inside a part-empty tank, leaking deck filler seals, rain or spray getting in while refuelling, and contaminated fuel from the supplier. Modern road diesel can contain a proportion of biodiesel, which holds more water than traditional diesel.

steps.title: The signs
steps.text: Dark slime or sludge in the primary filter bowl, filters that block much sooner than usual, and an engine that loses power or stops after rough weather has stirred up the bottom of the tank.

steps.title: Prevention
steps.text: Check the filler cap seal, drain the water trap regularly, buy fuel from a busy, reputable supplier, and refuel carefully in wet weather. What matters most is clean, dry fuel that is used and replaced regularly. Some owners keep the tank well filled over winter to limit condensation, while others prefer less fuel so that it does not go stale; follow your engine maker's and fuel supplier's guidance for your boat. Fuel additives such as biocides can help, but use them exactly as their maker directs.

steps.title: When it is bad
steps.text: If the tank is badly contaminated, additives alone will not fix it. The fuel may need to be filtered by a specialist fuel polishing service, or the tank emptied and cleaned.

lessons.reviewNote: Audit note 8, revise (S18): the lay-up advice no longer recommends full tanks; it stresses clean, dry fuel, water management, avoiding stale fuel and the maker's and supplier's guidance. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Why does the fuel pick-up pipe usually stop a little above the bottom of the tank?
options: So water and sludge that settle at the bottom are less likely to be drawn in
So that a reserve of fuel is kept back for emergencies
So the fuel stays warmer on its way to the engine in cold weather
So the tank vent cannot be blocked by fuel when the tank is full
questions.explanation: Water is heavier than diesel and dirt settles out, so both collect at the bottom of the tank. Drawing from slightly higher up keeps most of it out of the fuel system.

questions.prompt: Why does a small leak on the suction side of the fuel system often cause the engine to stop rather than drip fuel?
options: Because the suction draws air in through the leak instead of pushing fuel out
Because diesel evaporates from the joint before it has time to drip
Because the injection pump senses the leak and shuts the engine down to protect it
Because the return line keeps refilling the leak with fresh fuel
questions.explanation: Between the tank and the lift pump the fuel is under suction, so a loose joint pulls air in. That air reaches the injection pump, which cannot build pressure with air in it.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the fuel return or leak-off line?
options: To carry spare fuel, and any air it has picked up, back to the tank
To drain water from the bottom of the tank down into the primary filter bowl
To let air into the tank as the fuel level goes down
To carry fuel from the deck filler down into the tank
questions.explanation: The injection system is given more fuel than it burns. The surplus, along with any air bubbles, flows back to the tank. Letting air into the tank is the vent's job.

questions.prompt: Why can even a small bubble of air stop a diesel engine?
options: Air compresses, so the pump cannot build enough pressure to open the injectors
Air reacts with diesel in the lines and turns it into a thick wax
Air makes the fuel ignite too early, inside the lift pump itself
Air gets trapped in the filter element and blocks it completely
questions.explanation: Liquid fuel barely compresses, which is how the pump builds very high pressure. Air squashes like a spring instead, so the pressure needed to open the injector is not reached.

questions.prompt: Where does water collect in a primary fuel filter with a clear bowl?
options: At the bottom of the bowl, below the fuel
At the top of the bowl, floating above the fuel
Mixed evenly through the fuel
Soaked into the paper filter element
questions.explanation: Water is denser than diesel, so it sinks and forms a separate layer at the bottom of the bowl, where it can be seen and drained off.

questions.prompt: You see a layer of water in the primary filter bowl. What should you do?
options: With the engine stopped, drain it into a container until clean fuel runs out
Leave it there, because the engine's fine filter will catch it further along
Run the engine hard for an hour so that the water is burnt off
Drain it into the bilge so the bilge pump can take it away
questions.explanation: Water must be removed before it reaches the injection equipment. Drain it into a container, never into the bilge, because fuel-contaminated water must not be pumped overboard. Running the engine to 'burn off' water is not safe: water reaching the injection pump can damage it or stop the engine at sea.

questions.prompt: Why does a diesel engine have two stages of fuel filter?
options: The first catches water and larger dirt, so the finer second one can take out tiny particles
The second filter is a spare that only starts working if the first one becomes blocked
One filter cleans the fuel going to the engine and the other cleans fuel returning to the tank
Two filters let the engine run on two different grades of fuel without any changes
questions.explanation: Removing the water and bigger particles first protects the fine filter, which then takes out the very small particles that would damage the injection pump and injectors.

questions.prompt: After changing a fuel filter element, what will the engine usually need before it runs properly?
options: The fuel system bled to remove the air let in
A new set of injectors fitted and pressure tested
The engine oil and oil filter changed
The raw water strainer cleaned out
questions.explanation: Opening a filter lets air into the fuel system. Unless the engine is self-bleeding, that air must be pushed out before the injection pump can work.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of the lift pump?
options: To draw fuel from the tank and feed it to the injection pump
To spray a fine mist of fuel into each of the cylinders
To pump any water out of the bottom of the fuel tank
To raise the fuel to the very high pressure needed for injection
questions.explanation: The lift pump works on the low-pressure side, keeping the injection pump supplied. Creating the very high injection pressure is the injection pump's job.

questions.prompt: How are many mechanically injected small marine diesels stopped?
options: By cutting off the fuel at the injection pump
By switching off the glow plugs
By closing the fuel valve at the tank
By switching off the battery isolator
questions.explanation: The stop control, a cable or solenoid, shuts off fuel delivery at the injection pump. Closing the tank valve would take a long time and lets air in, glow plugs only help starting, and switching off the isolator with the engine running can damage the alternator. Electronically controlled engines are stopped through their control system.
questions.reviewNote: Audit note 5, revise: the question now says 'many mechanically injected' engines, with credible distractors and a warning about the isolator in the explanation. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Why should you never feel for a leak along a high-pressure fuel pipe with your hand?
options: The fuel is under enough pressure to pierce skin and cause serious injury
The pipes carry an electrical current while the engine is running, as part of the stop circuit
Oils from your skin make the steel fuel pipes corrode quickly
The pipe can crack if it is touched while the engine is running
questions.explanation: A fine jet of fuel from a high-pressure leak can be injected through the skin. This is a medical emergency, so look for leaks visually or with a piece of card instead.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a typical sign of a faulty injector?
options: Black smoke and rough running, sometimes with a knock from one cylinder
Black smoke only at full load that clears once the air filter is changed
Blue smoke that gets worse after long periods at idle
Steam and very little water coming out of the exhaust
questions.explanation: An injector that dribbles or sprays poorly delivers fuel that does not burn completely, giving smoke, rough running and sometimes a knock. Black smoke cured by a new air filter points to the air supply, blue smoke to oil, and steam to cooling.

questions.prompt: With the engine running, you see a fine mist of fuel around one of the injector pipes. What should you do?
options: Stop and check the handbook; leave the high-pressure side to an engineer
Loosen it slightly while someone cranks, to see whether fuel spurts out
Open it, because owners can safely bleed at any connection on a fuel system
Feel along the pipe while the engine turns to see whether it is under pressure
questions.explanation: Fuel from a high-pressure leak can be injected through the skin, and the spray is a fire risk. Stop the engine, keep clear, contain any spill and do not restart until a qualified engineer has repaired it. Suspected injection injury needs emergency medical treatment.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.1 (S20): a safety-first scenario question on fuel spray, matching the Fault finder stop card. Please approve.

questions.prompt: Which of these usually means the fuel system will need bleeding?
options: The engine ran out of fuel
The engine oil was changed
The alternator belt was adjusted
The raw water impeller was replaced
questions.explanation: Running the tank dry lets air into the fuel lines. Oil changes, belt work and impeller changes do not open the fuel system.

questions.prompt: In what order should you work through the bleed points?
options: From the point nearest the tank towards the engine, following the fuel's path
From the injectors back towards the tank, against the fuel's flow
In any order you like, as long as every bleed point gets opened
All the points opened at once, then closed together at the end
questions.explanation: Fuel pushes air ahead of it along the system. Starting near the tank clears each section in turn; starting at the far end just draws more air through from behind.

questions.prompt: When should you close a bleed screw?
options: While fuel free of bubbles is still flowing out
As soon as the first drop of fuel appears
After the pump has stopped and fuel has stopped flowing
Only once the engine has started
questions.explanation: Closing while clean fuel is still flowing stops air being drawn back in. The first drops often still carry bubbles, so keep pumping until they stop.

questions.prompt: The hand lever on a cam-operated mechanical lift pump has almost no movement. What is a likely reason?
options: The engine's cam is holding the pump's arm at the top of its travel
The fuel valve at the tank has been left closed
The primary filter is blocked, so the pump cannot draw fuel
The lift pump's diaphragm has split
questions.explanation: A mechanical lift pump is worked by a cam on the engine. If the engine stopped with the cam lobe holding the arm, the hand lever has little travel; turning the engine a little frees it. A closed valve, blocked filter or split diaphragm stops fuel flowing but does not usually stop the lever moving. Electric lift pumps have no lever.
questions.reviewNote: Audit note 7, accept with qualification: the question now names cam-operated mechanical pumps, and the explanation says electric pumps differ. Please approve.

questions.prompt: You bleed the system, the engine runs for a few minutes, then stops again with the same symptoms. What should you suspect?
options: Air is still getting in somewhere, so the cause has not been found
The engine needs a higher grade of oil before it will keep running for long
The bleeding was done while the engine was too cold
The injection pump was damaged when the tank ran dry
questions.explanation: Bleeding removes air but does not stop it entering. If air returns, look for a loose joint, a damaged seal, a split hose on the suction side or a low tank.

questions.prompt: While bleeding, you are not sure whether the next connection is on the low-pressure or the high-pressure side. What should you do?
options: Stop and check the handbook, and leave anything on the high-pressure side to a qualified engineer
Loosen it slightly while someone cranks, to see whether fuel spurts out
Open it, because owners can safely bleed at any connection on a fuel system
Feel along the pipe while the engine turns to see whether it is under pressure
questions.explanation: Owner bleeding is limited to the handbook's low-pressure points. High-pressure fuel can penetrate skin and cause severe injury, so if you are unsure, stop and check, and use a qualified engineer for anything else.
questions.reviewNote: New in content 1.1 (S02, S20): a safety-first question on the low-pressure boundary, with warning B in the feedback. Please approve.

questions.prompt: What is diesel bug?
options: Micro-organisms that grow where water meets fuel in the tank, forming sludge
A wax that forms in diesel fuel, but only during very cold weather in winter
An insect that gets into fuel tanks through the breather vent
A fault in the injection pump's electronic control unit
questions.explanation: Bacteria and fungi live at the boundary between water and fuel. They feed on the fuel and form a slime that blocks filters. Cold-weather waxing is a separate problem.

questions.prompt: Why do engines with fuel contamination often stop in rough weather?
options: The motion stirs up water and sludge from the tank bottom, which blocks the filters
Waves force diesel out of the tank through the vent, so it runs low
The injection pump cannot work properly when the boat heels over
Cold spray thickens the fuel in the lines until it can no longer flow
questions.explanation: In calm conditions, dirt and water sit undisturbed below the pick-up. Rough water churns them into the fuel, and the filters block soon afterwards.

questions.prompt: Which of these helps most to stop water getting into the fuel tank?
options: Keeping the deck filler cap seal in good condition
Adding a biocide every time you refuel
Draining the primary filter bowl more often
Fitting a second fine filter on the engine
questions.explanation: A worn filler seal lets rain and spray straight into the tank. A biocide treats the effects of water, draining the bowl removes water that has already got in, and an extra filter does nothing to keep it out.

questions.prompt: A tank is badly contaminated with diesel bug. Why are additives alone not enough?
options: They may kill the organisms, but the existing sludge stays and keeps blocking filters
Additives are designed for petrol engines and have no effect in diesel
Additives make the fuel too thick for the lift pump to draw it
Additives only start to work once the engine runs at full power for hours
questions.explanation: A biocide can stop further growth, but the dead sludge remains and will still block filters. A badly affected tank needs the fuel polished or the tank cleaned.
